sources.news_title: Trump announces Karoline Leavitt's departure as White House press secretary
sources.text:
Rabia Iclal Turan
12 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced that White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her role at the end of August and become one of his top outside advisers. 
“Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect,” Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social. 
He said Leavitt would remain “an influential voice within the Republican Party” as the party works to “conclusively win the Midterm Elections,” which are less than three months away, on Nov. 3.  
Trump is not on the ballot for the midterms, but if Democrats make sizeable gains in Congress, as most current polls predict, Trump’s ability to govern in the rest of his term could be significantly hindered. 
Writing on US social media company X, Leavitt said: “Being a mother and welcoming a new baby while working in one of the most demanding jobs in the world has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life, to say the least." 
"The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary — and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life," she said. 
"President Trump has asked me to continue serving as a top advisor to him on the outside, and I will always remain a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party," she added, referring to Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan. 
"It has been a privilege to serve alongside so many accomplished and impressive people, and I look forward to cheering them on over the next two and a half years." 
Leavitt, 28, became the youngest White House press secretary in US history when Trump named her to the post in November 2024. 
She previously served as an assistant press secretary during Trump’s first term and as national press secretary for his 2024 campaign to return to the White House. 
Leavitt began her maternity leave in April and gave birth to her second child, a daughter named Viviana, on May 1. She and her husband, Nicholas Riccio, also have a son born in 2024.

sources.news_title: Karoline Leavitt abruptly quits White House in shock departure announced by Trump
sources.text:
Karoline Leavitt is leaving the White House.
President Donald Trump announced Wednesday that his press secretary will step down from her post at the end of the month, marking a surprise departure for one of the most visible and combative members of his administration.
Trump broke the news in a Truth Social post, praising Leavitt as his “wonderful White House Press Secretary” and one of his “most trusted aides.”
“Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family,” Trump wrote, adding that it was a decision he “totally understand[s] and respect[s].”
But Leavitt isn’t exactly disappearing from Trump world.
Trump said she will continue working as one of his “top outside” advisers and will remain an influential voice in the Republican Party as the midterm elections approach.
Leavitt confirmed the decision in a post on X, describing her time as press secretary as “the honor and adventure of a lifetime.”
But she said becoming a mother for the second time changed the equation.
“The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary,” Leavitt wrote.
She called the decision “bittersweet” and said she was ready to begin a new chapter.
Politically, however, Leavitt isn’t going anywhere.
She pledged to remain a vocal supporter of Trump, MAGA and the Republican Party, saying the president had asked her to continue serving as an outside adviser heading into the midterms.
“Our country is facing an existential threat from an increasingly extremist Democrat Party that seeks to destroy everything great about America,” Leavitt wrote. “My fight is entering a new phase, but it is far from over.”
Leavitt has been one of the most recognizable faces of the Trump administration, particularly during the often-combative White House press briefings.
Her relationship with Trump goes back years.
She served as an assistant press secretary during Trump’s first administration from 2019 to 2021. After Trump left office, she became communications director for Rep. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y.
In 2022, Leavitt launched a campaign for New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District. She won the Republican nomination but ultimately lost to Democratic incumbent Chris Pappas.
She later joined Trump’s political operation, becoming a spokesperson for his super PAC MAGA Inc. before moving onto his 2024 presidential campaign.
After Trump won, he selected Leavitt to become his press secretary.
At just 27 years old, she became the youngest person ever to hold the position.
She quickly developed a reputation for an aggressive liar, unapologetically pro-Trump style at the briefing room podium and became an important part of Trump’s inner circle.
Leavitt also made history in 2025 when she announced she was pregnant with her second child, becoming the first sitting White House press secretary to serve while pregnant.
She went on maternity leave in May and returned to the podium in July.
Now, just weeks after returning, she’s preparing to leave the White House again.
Officially, Leavitt says the reason is family.
But politically, she’s not walking away from Trump. She’s simply moving outside the building.

WASHINGTON — White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her position at the end of August to spend more time with her family, President Donald Trump announced on social media Wednesday.
In a post on Truth Social, the president praised Leavitt, the youngest person to serve in the role, as one of his closest aides in the White House and said she will move to an adviser role outside of government.
“Our wonderful White House Press Secretary, and one of my most trusted aides, Karoline Leavitt, will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect!” Trump wrote.
“Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections,” he added.
When asked whether the White House had chosen the next press secretary, a spokesperson pointed States Newsroom to Trump’s and Leavitt’s social media posts and did not provide additional comment.
In a nearly 500-word statement on the social media platform X, Leavitt thanked the president “for granting me so many extraordinary opportunities,” which she said included spending “countless hours” in the Oval Office and meeting foreign leaders and Americans “from all walks of life.”
“Most of all, I am thankful to the President for entrusting me with the distinct privilege of speaking on his behalf at the White House podium. I have spoken with great pride about the many historic accomplishments of this Administration, and I have relished holding the liberal media accountable and ensuring the American people hear the truth about President Trump’s successes,” said Leavitt, who was at times combative with journalists during routine press briefings.
Leavitt gave birth to her second child on May 1, and held her first briefing following parental leave less than a month ago. She described her decision to leave “one of the most demanding jobs in the world” as “bittersweet.”
Leavitt said she will “always remain a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party” and suggested she’d continue antagonizing the president’s political opponents.
“Our country is facing an existential threat from an increasingly extremist Democrat Party that seeks to destroy everything great about America, and I believe it is incumbent upon all of us who care about this country to fight back against that threat,” she wrote.
Leavitt credited White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, who co-managed Trump’s 2024 re-election bid, for initially hiring her during the campaign.
Leavitt was 27 years old when she assumed the role of press secretary in January 2025.

sources.news_title: Karoline Leavitt quits as Trump's Press Secretary, will be his outside adviser
sources.text:
Karoline Leavitt quits as Trump's Press Secretary, will be his outside adviser
Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person ever to hold the high-profile post, said she was leaving the demanding White House job to spend more time with her two children.
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down at the end of August, but will continue working with President Donald Trump as an outside adviser. Leavitt, the youngest person ever to hold the high-profile post, said she was leaving the demanding White House job to spend more time with her two children.
During her 18 months in office, Leavitt, 28, earned a reputation as a staunch Trump loyalist, while also becoming known for fiery clashes with reporters during White House briefings.
She gave birth to her second child, a daughter, in May and had recently returned to the White House following maternity leave.
In a post on X, Leavitt, a fierce Trump backer, described her time as Press Secretary as “the honour and adventure of a lifetime” but said balancing motherhood with one of the administration's most demanding jobs had become increasingly difficult.
She said that after returning to work following her daughter's birth, she realised she could not be the mother she wanted to be while continuing to devote the “constant time, energy and attention” the Press Secretary's job requires.
Leavitt is expected to remain involved in Trump's political operation after leaving the White House, serving as an outside communications adviser and continuing to work with the broader “Make America Great Again” movement.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump praised Leavitt's performance, describing her as “one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office”. He said she had been a leader in his administration and had played an important role in his 2024 re-election campaign.
"Karoline has been a real leader in the White House, and has done a phenomenal job fighting for Justice, Liberty, and Freedom, since 2018, including our Historic Re-Election Campaign of 2024," he said.
YOUNGEST PRESS SECRETARY
Leavitt joined Trump's 2024 presidential campaign and later served as its transition spokesperson before being chosen to lead the White House press operation. At 26, she became the youngest person ever appointed White House press secretary when she took office in January 2025.
Her tenure coincided with a significant overhaul of the White House's relationship with the news media. Working alongside White House communications director Steven Cheung, Leavitt helped implement changes that gave the administration greater control over which journalists received access to the president.
The White House also moved away from the traditional system in which the White House Correspondents' Association determined the rotating press pool. The administration instead gave greater access to podcasts, newsletters and newer digital outlets, creating a dedicated “new media” seat in the briefing room.
Trump's supporters welcomed the changes as an adaptation to a changing media environment, while press freedom advocates argued that the new system could allow the administration to favour outlets that offered more sympathetic coverage.
Leavitt's departure comes as the administration faces scrutiny over a reported security operation during Trump's visit to a NATO summit in Turkey in July.
The Washington Post reported this week that the Secret Service moved Trump between aircraft in a catering truck while journalists and staff remained aboard another plane, amid concerns about a possible Iranian assassination threat.
The reported move represented a break from the usual practice of ensuring that journalists travelling with the president are aware of his movements.

sources.news_title: Karoline Leavitt will tell her last lie from the White House podium this month. Trump says she's leaving
sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced Wednesday afternoon that White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her post at the end of August, closing a tenure in which the administration’s youngest-ever chief spokesperson became one of its most aggressive defenders — including when the facts did not support what she was saying and when transgender Americans were the target.
Trump announced Leavitt’s departure on Truth Social shortly after 3:30 p.m., saying the 28-year-old wanted to spend more time with her two young children. She recently returned from maternity leave after giving birth to her second child in May. Leavitt is married to Nicholas Riccio, a 60-year-old New Hampshire real estate developer—the couple, who have a 32-year age gap, married in January 2025. Trump said Leavitt would remain “one of my top outside advisors” as Republicans approach the midterm elections. He has not named her successor.
Related: Trump’s new White House Press Secretary targets transgender people in first briefing
“Karoline has been one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office,” Trump wrote.
Independent fact-checkers documented a considerably less flattering record.
At Leavitt’s first briefing in January 2025, she promised to “provide the truth” from the podium. She then claimed the Biden administration had been preparing to spend $50 million on condoms in Gaza, for which the administration provided no evidence. PolitiFact rated the claim false.
In March, Leavitt declared that “tariffs are a tax cut for the American people.” PolitiFact rated that false, noting tariffs are taxes imposed on imported goods, and their costs can be passed along to U.S. consumers. Two months later, the organization again rated Leavitt false after she claimed Trump’s tax and spending legislation “does not add to the deficit.”
Leavitt also became a reliable public voice for an administration carrying out a sweeping assault on trans rights.
From her first briefing, she celebrated Trump’s order directing the federal government to recognize only male and female sexes and disparaged federal spending related to “transgenderism and wokeness.” She repeatedly defended Trump administration efforts restricting transgender participation in sports and access to gender-affirming care.
One particularly revealing episode came in August 2025, after Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, the out gay director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, resigned amid turmoil at the agency. Daskalakis warned in his resignation letter that changes to vaccine policy threatened “the youngest Americans and pregnant people.” Leavitt seized not on his warnings about public health but on those final two words.
“One of those individuals wrote in his departure statement that he identifies pregnant women as pregnant people,” Leavitt told reporters. “So that’s not someone who we want in this administration anyway.”
Daskalakis later told The Advocate that his wording was intentional and connected Leavitt’s attack to the administration’s treatment of transgender people. “I accept the note, and I don’t care,” he said.
Leavitt’s tenure was also marked by an extraordinary White House effort to exert greater control over the journalists covering the presidency. In February 2025, after the Associated Press refused to adopt Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America” terminology for the Gulf of Mexico, the White House barred AP journalists from some presidential events. Leavitt then announced that her press office, rather than the independent White House Correspondents’ Association, would decide which news organizations participated in the presidential press pool — stripping the journalists’ organization of a role it had performed for generations.
Related: Karoline Leavitt: Trump wants 'less LGBTQ graduate majors' from Harvard
The WHCA warned that allowing the government to choose the reporters who cover it threatened the independence of the press.
The administration went further in April, eliminating the permanent pool positions traditionally held by the AP, Reuters and Bloomberg and reserving day-to-day discretion over who would get access. The WHCA called the policy another way to “retaliate against news organizations for coverage the White House doesn’t like.” Leavitt portrayed the broader shake-up differently, opening a “new media” seat in the briefing room to podcasters, influencers and other digital creators and arguing that the White House was adapting to the way Americans consume news.
“Thank you, Karoline, for a job well done!” Trump wrote.

sources.news_title: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt leaves position to spend time with family
sources.text:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her role at the end of the month, US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday, leaving the president without one of his most trusted advisers ahead of November's midterm elections.
Leavitt will be an outside communications adviser and party operative shaping the future contours of Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement, she and Trump said in statements.
In a social media post, Leavitt, 28, said she aimed to spend more time with her young children. She gave birth to a daughter, her second child, in May and recently returned from maternity leave.
"Karoline has been a real leader in the White House, and has done a phenomenal job fighting for Justice, Liberty, and Freedom, since 2018, including our Historic Re-Election Campaign of 2024," Trump said in a social media post, calling Leavitt "one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office."
Leavitt called her role at the White House "the honor and adventure of a lifetime."
Leavitt is youngest ever White House press secretary
Leavitt joined Trump's 2024 campaign and served as transition spokeswoman before Trump selected her to be White House press secretary. She was the youngest person to be appointed to the role.
"Few could or will ever compare to Karoline," said Harrison Fields, Trump's former principal deputy press secretary. "She's someone who not only spoke Trump fluently, she knew how to feed the media beast in a cunning, audacious, and successful way that, most importantly, played to her audience: the president."
In her year and a half on the job, Leavitt and White House communications director Steven Cheung transformed the administration's posture toward the media - in ways that some of Trump's allies cheered and free press advocates criticized.
The Trump administration began handpicking which journalists receive access to the president, jettisoning the long-running system set up by the independent White House Correspondents Association. The "press pool" was traditionally a rotation chosen by the industry group to ensure media outlets had uniform access to the president and could relay his activities to the public and to other journalists who could not attend smaller gatherings.
As part of that process, the Trump administration press office created a special "new media" seat in the briefing room that gave podcasts, newsletters and fledgling digital outlets a more prominent role in covering the presidency. Some press advocates hailed the move as a recognition of the changing media landscape. Others criticized it as a lever the administration could use to reward outlets whose coverage it saw as favorable.
Leavitt's post one of Washington's most demanding
Although Leavitt is leaving the White House less than two years after taking the job, her tenure is not unusually short by modern standards. The White House press secretary is one of Washington’s most demanding and highly scrutinized positions, and in recent decades many have served for roughly a year and a half to three years.
Jen Psaki, former president Joe Biden’s first press secretary, left after about 16 months; Jay Carney served for roughly three and a half years under Barack Obama, while Josh Earnest held the job for about two and a half years.
Some of the notable exceptions date to earlier administrations: James Hagerty served for nearly all eight years of Dwight Eisenhower’s presidency, while Marlin Fitzwater served under two presidents, Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush.
Leavitt’s tenure, which will total approximately 19 months by the time she departs at the end of August, therefore falls comfortably within the modern pattern for one of the White House’s most relentless public-facing jobs.

WASHINGTON – White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her role at the end of the month, US President Donald Trump said on Aug 12, leaving the President without one of his most trusted advisers ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Leavitt will be an outside communications adviser and party operative shaping the future contours of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, she and Trump said in statements.

“Karoline has been a real leader in the White House, and has done a phenomenal job fighting for justice, liberty, and freedom, since 2018, including our historic re-election campaign of 2024,” Trump said in a social media post, calling Leavitt “one of the best White House press secretaries in the history of the Office”.
Leavitt called her role at the White House “the honour and adventure of a lifetime”.
Youngest White House press secretary
Leavitt joined Trump’s 2024 campaign and served as transition spokeswoman before Trump selected her to be White House press secretary. She was the youngest person to be appointed to the role.
“Few could or will ever compare to Karoline,” said Harrison Fields, Trump’s former principal deputy press secretary. “She’s someone who not only spoke Trump fluently, she knew how to feed the media beast in a cunning, audacious and successful way that, most importantly, played to her audience: the President.”
In her year and a half on the job, Leavitt and White House communications director Steven Cheung transformed the administration’s posture towards the media – in ways that some of Trump’s allies cheered and free press advocates criticised.
The Trump administration began handpicking which journalists receive access to the President, jettisoning the long-running system set up by the independent White House Correspondents’ Association.
The “press pool” was traditionally a rotation chosen by the industry group to ensure media outlets had uniform access to the president and could relay his activities to the public and to other journalists who could not attend smaller gatherings.
As part of that process, the Trump administration press office created a special “new media” seat in the briefing room that gave podcasts, newsletters and fledgling digital outlets a more prominent role in covering the presidency.
Some press advocates hailed the move as a recognition of the changing media landscape. Others criticised it as a lever the administration could use to reward outlets whose coverage it saw as favourable. REUTERS

sources.text:
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt will leave her post at the end of August, President Donald Trump announced Tuesday, citing a desire from the 28-year-old to spend more time with her two young children after recently returning from maternity leave.
Trump broke the news in a post on Truth Social, praising Leavitt as “one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office” and confirming she would not be leaving the administration’s orbit entirely.

Leavitt’s exit marks one of the most notable staff departures of Trump’s second term to date, coming at a moment when the administration has faced an unusually heavy volume of high-profile news cycles, from foreign policy flashpoints to domestic legal battles, that have kept the press secretary’s role squarely in the public eye. Her ability to manage that pace from the podium had drawn consistent praise from Trump and senior officials, who credited her with sharpening the administration’s rapid-response media strategy.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced Wednesday afternoon on Truth Social that Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt “will be departing her role at the end of the month,” capping an incredible run that revolutionized the White House press briefing to democratize the voices in the Brady Briefing Room and bring this normally elitist, liberal confab closer to the people.
A mother to a two-year-old and three-month-old, the President said she’ll be leaving to “spend more time with her beautiful young children and family,” but remain “one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party.”
The President said he “totally understand[s] and respect[s]” her decision, adding she will help the GOP “defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.”
Trump concluded:
Karoline has been a real leader in the White House, and has done a phenomenal job fighting for Justice, Liberty, and Freedom, since 2018, including our Historic Re-Election Campaign of 2024. Karoline has been one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office. Thank you, Karoline, for a job well done!
Regardless of her exact date of departure, Leavitt will have concluded the second-longest-run for anyone to serve in this crucial role at the pleasure of this President, topped only by now-Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders (who served 20 days shy of two years).
For her part, Leavitt posted on X that the role “has been the honor and adventure of a lifetime,” and that’s “incredibly grateful to President Trump for granting me so many extraordinary opportunities, such as working in the West Wing and spending countless hours in the Oval Office, flying around the world and meeting foreign leaders, and traveling across our beautiful country and meeting Americans from all walks of life.”
Leavitt added she’s “relished holding the liberal media accountable and ensuring the American people hear the truth about President Trump’s successes” through “the distinct privilege of speaking on his behalf at the White House podium.”
Leavitt confirmed the reason for her departure, explaining that, “since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary[.]”
Later, she offered a series of thanks and expanded on the importance of her new, undefined role: “President Trump has asked me to continue serving as a top advisor to him on the outside, and I will always remain a vocal advocate for MAGA and the Republican Party...My fight is entering a new phase, but it is far from over,” she said, addressing her new, undefined role.
Leavitt announced in her first briefing on January 28, 2025, that it would be a new era in the Briefing Room with the creation of a “new media” seat, and invited bloggers, influencers, and independent journalists to apply for consideration. This would later cause outlets such as The New York Times to pitch hissy fits.
She also was known for crisp, tight briefings of well under an hour, and calling on an expansive number of reporters. In that January briefing, for example, she called on 21 reporters credentialed with 20 different outlets.
Nearly a month later, on February 25, 2025, Leavitt shared another monumental change as she said the White House Communications Office — not the White House Correspondents Association (WHCA) — would be taking over press pool assignments (meaning, the small band of reporters that travel with the President or attend events in tighter confines, such as the Oval Office).
Unsurprisingly, this created some cataclysmic meltdowns on the part of legacy media, fearing their access would be ripped away and be entirely replaced by Trump sycophants. In actuality, Leavitt and her team expanded the pool.
While continuing to rotate the TV crew between the six networks (ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC), they instituted a spot for a second TV correspondent that allowed organizations such as NewsNation and Newsmax to join the pool when, under past presidents, they had been excluded.
As part of that, the Associated Press lost its consistent presence in the pool over its refusal to use the term “Gulf of America,” causing a whole other set of hand-wringing. Eventually, the AP returned to the pool.
Leavitt was also not afraid to use the Briefing Room podium to name names when it came to media misconduct.
Whether it was MSNBC’s Nicolle Wallace, CNN’s Natasha Bertrand, the BBC, CNN Business, CNN’s Kaitlan Collins (more than a few times), The Hill’s Niall Stanage, The New York Times’s Katie Rogers, or the press’s repeated pro-Iranian tendencies to name a few, Leavitt represented President Trump well and was not there to schmooze or ingratiate herself to the far-left media class.

sources.text:
Trump says White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her position at the end of the month, President Donald Trump has announced.
Leavitt, whom the president called one of his "most trusted aides", will depart from her role to spend time with her young children and family - "a decision I totally understand and respect", Trump wrote in a social media post.
"Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," he added.
Leavitt, 28, took the job as White House Press Secretary last year - becoming the youngest person to ever have the role. It was not immediately clear who will replace her.
Leavitt welcomed her second child, a baby girl, with husband Nicholas Riccio in May. She also has a two-year-old son. She returned to work from maternity leave last month.
She wrote on X following the president's announcement that her job has been "the honor and adventure of a lifetime".
"Being a mother and welcoming a new baby while working in one of the most demanding jobs in the world has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life, to say the least," she wrote.
"The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary - and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life," she continued.
Before her tenure at the White House as press secretary, she had a long career working with Trump, first as an assistant press secretary and speech writer during his first term in office.
She later went on to become a top aide to New York Republican congresswoman Elise Stefanik as communications director.
In 2022, Leavitt unsuccessfully ran for Congress in New Hampshire, emerging victorious from a contested Republican primary, but ultimately losing to Democrat Chris Pappas.
She later became a spokesperson for Maga Inc - a pro-Trump fundraising group - before joining his 2024 electoral campaign as national press secretary.
Leavitt has had a sometimes combative relationship with the media during her tenure, accusing some reporters of being biased or left-wing.
In February last year, her office seized control of the White House press pool, stripping organisational duties from the White House Correspondent's Association, as well as initially barring the Associated Press over its refusal to adopt the term "Gulf of America".
Among supporters of the Trump administration, however, she was widely praised for remaining "on message" and ferociously defending the president's policies.
"Watching it in person was even better than watching it online," Fox host and conservative activist Riley Gaines wrote on X after one particularly feisty briefing room exchange. "Karoline Leavitt is so good at her job."
She is the second longest-serving press secretary in either of Trump's administrations, following only Sarah Huckabee Sanders.
It is unclear who will now become Trump's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations.
During Leavitt's roughly seven-week maternity leave earlier this year, a series of senior Trump administration figures took the podium including Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Secretary of the Interior Doug Bergum.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on potential choices and the timeline of her replacement's selection.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller - who called Leavitt a "close friend" and "role model".
"We're going to continue working together every single day," he added. "Her story is just beginning. I can't wait to see what her future holds."

Leavitt, who gave birth to her daughter Viviana in May and returned from maternity leave last month, confirmed the decision on X. She wrote, “The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life.”
Leavitt served as a press aide during Trump’s first term, ran for Congress in New Hampshire in 2022 and served as spokeswoman for Trump’s 2024 campaign and transition team. At 27, she became the youngest person to hold the press secretary role.
Trump previously praised her performance during an interview, stating, “She’s become a star. It’s that face, it’s that brain, it’s those lips – the way they move, they move like she’s a machine gun.”
The announcement comes after reports revealed that officials used White House staff and journalists as unwitting decoys aboard Air Force One.
Security officials secretly moved Trump off Air Force One using an airport catering container in Turkiye and flew him to Britain on a military C-32A jet due to a credible threat from Iran. The older Air Force One, carrying staff and press, flew to Britain as a decoy.
Social media users immediately linked the decoy operation to the resignation, pointing out that Leavitt announced her exit 24 hours after learning she was left on a plane officials thought could be shot down.
Reactions flooded platforms, with one user writing, “Jeez Karoline, really sorry that the man you lied for constantly and sold your soul to, didn’t care enough about you to inform you that you could have been killed, leaving your tiny children without a mother.”
Another commenter added, “What do you mean? A narcissist only thought of himself and none of the people who have been (erroneously) loyal to him? That’s quite a surprise.”
Others focused on her role defending the administration, with one post stating, “Leavitt’s biggest mistake? Thinking she could defend a man who lies more than he breathes. That’s not a job, that’s a suicide mission.”
Additional users speculated on the timing, writing that she had to deport before she departed, while another noted, “I’m sure it’s just a coincidence that Karoline Leavitt resigned as White House press secretary after being an unwitting decoy on Air Force One.”
Sarcastic comments also emerged, with one post asking if she was “Jealous she didn’t get to ride in the catering truck” while another noted: “Kinda hits you in the boo boo when the world finds out that your boss hung you out for bait!”
Political figures offered opposing reactions to her departure. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum praised her on social media, writing, “Karoline Leavitt has served President Trump and the American people with courage and conviction. She’s a great colleague, a fearless voice for the President’s agenda and a true professional.”
California Senator Adam Schiff presented a contrasting view on X, writing, “Karoline Leavitt is leaving the White House to spend a little more time … with the truth.”
